newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Pearson accounting problem at Penguin.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pearson accounting problem at Penguin.

text.p: British media group Pearson Plc shocked the market on Thursday, saying that improper accounting at its Penguin USA books unit would force it to make a charge of up to 100 million pounds ($163 million) against 1996 profits.
The news of what one analyst called "quite a horrific provision" initially sent Pearson shares into a tailspin.

They fell by more than nine percent at one point to 690 pence, before rallying strongly to to 751-1/2 for a loss of 12p by 1230 GMT as analysts said the news rekindled the view that the group was a candidate for a takeover bid.
"The more they (Pearson) disappoint, the more people expect someone to bid for them," analyst Anthony de Larrinaga of Panmure Gordon said.

Pearson said in a statement the problems, which date back to 1991 but only emerged very recently, arose from unauthorised discounting of invoices for early payment by customers, with the discounts not fully recognised in Penguin USA's accounts.

The complex nature of publishers' accounts, with hundreds of thousands of transactions passing through the New-York based Penguin USA's New Jersey facility where its accounting operations are, made it easier for a what a Pearson spokesman called a "very determined individual" to conceal the discrepancies.
"I think we are dealing with a very determined individual," the spokesman said.

"We are confident we have provided for not only what we have discovered so far but also what will be discovered (as the investigation continues to its conclusion)," the spokesman said, describing the likely provisions as conservative.
Pearson said that those found to be responsible for the problem, "have been and will be appropriately dealt with", without giving details.

Marjorie Scardino, who took over as Pearson chief executive at the start of the year, said in the statement, "We have moved quickly to implement a detailed plan of action to address these unauthorised practices."

De Larrinaga said the news showed Scardino and her new team were "tightening up", but said it highlighted the problems she faces in tackling Pearson's woes, as well as asking serious questions of management controls.

The problems were uncovered by Michael Lynton, who took over as Penguin chairman and chief executive in January, and his management team, and are being investigated by lawyers and by accountants Price Waterhouse.
Lynton and finance director John Makinson will keep Scardino informed. "I will get on with running the Group," she said.
Pearson said the profits of Penguin would not be restated and Pearson has not changed its 1997 profit expectations for the company as a result of the unauthorised discounts.
The scale of the provisions compare with 1996 gross sales at Penguin USA -- before allowances for books returned -- of 300 million pounds.
Scardino, a Texan who came to the top job at Pearson from its 50-percent owned Economist magazine business, has said that Pearson's profit performance is not good enough.
Another analyst, while describing Pearson's profit record over the past six or seven years as "dire", said the market awaits full details of the events in New Jersey.
He said although thoughts of a bid remained "in the back of people's minds", investors would grant the new management team a period in which to bring about improvement at the company.

Media reports have periodically raised the possibility of a break up of the company, whose interests span the Financial Times, television, Madame Tussaud's waxworks, banking and the troubled U.S. consumer software company Mindscape, with BSkyB and possibly U.S. media groups interested in its assets.

Pearson is due to announce its 1996 results on March 18, when analysts hope to hear something of the new team's restructuring plans. Pre-tax profits, before the Penguin USA provision, are forecast at between 235 and 290 million pounds, down from 365.1 million in 1995.
